content: Adalimumab is indicated for the treatment of moderate-to-severe active rheumatoid arthritis at a dose of 40 mg administered subcutaneously every two weeks. It is also indicated for the treatment of active psoriatic arthritis at the same dose and frequency. For active ankylosing spondylitis, it is used to reduce signs and symptoms at a dose of 40 mg subcutaneously every two weeks. For moderate-to-severe chronic plaque psoriasis in patients who are candidates for systemic therapy or phototherapy, and when systemic therapies are inappropriate, the initial dose is 80 mg subcutaneously once, followed by 40 mg subcutaneously every two weeks starting one week later. However, the use of adalimumab in chronic plaque psoriasis beyond one year has not been evaluated in controlled clinical studies. The prescribing information includes data on patients with moderate-to-severe fingernail psoriasis. Adalimumab is indicated for the reduction of signs and symptoms, as well as the induction and maintenance of clinical remission, in patients with moderately-to-severely active Crohn’s disease who have had an inadequate response to conventional therapy. It may also be used in patients who have lost response to or are intolerant of infliximab. The induction regimen involves 160 mg subcutaneously (administered as four 40 mg injections on day 1 or two 40 mg injections daily on two consecutive days), followed by 80 mg subcutaneously two weeks later (day 15). Maintenance therapy begins at week 4 (day 29) with 40 mg subcutaneously every two weeks. Continued maintenance dosing is recommended only if clinical remission is evident by eight weeks of therapy. Effectiveness in Crohn’s disease beyond one year has not been established in controlled clinical studies. It is also indicated for patients unresponsive to immunosuppressants such as corticosteroids, azathioprine, or 6-mercaptopurine. Adalimumab is indicated for the treatment of moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa (Hurley stage 2 and 3 disease) in adults and adolescents aged 12 years or older who weigh at least 30 kg. For noninfectious intermediate, posterior, and panuveitis in adults, the initial dose is 80 mg subcutaneously once, followed by 40 mg subcutaneously every two weeks starting one week later. It has orphan designation for the treatment of Behçet’s disease. Adalimumab is interchangeable with biosimilars such as Cyltezo and Amjevita. It is indicated for the reduction of signs and symptoms of moderately-to-severely active polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. It may be administered with methotrexate, glucocorticoids, NSAIDs, or analgesics. Safety and efficacy have not been established in children under two years of age or weighing less than 10 kg. In pediatric patients with moderately-to-severely active Crohn’s disease who have had an inadequate response to corticosteroids or immunomodulators (e.g., azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate), adalimumab is indicated to reduce signs and symptoms and achieve and maintain clinical remission. Safety and efficacy have not been established in children under six years of age. Adalimumab is indicated for moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis in patients aged five years or older. Safety and efficacy have not been established in children under five years of age. It is also indicated for noninfectious intermediate, posterior, and panuveitis in patients aged two years or older. Safety and efficacy have not been established in children under two years of age or weighing less than 10 kg. Adalimumab interacts with various drugs and vaccines, often increasing the risk of serious infections due to its immunosuppressive effects. It is contraindicated with live vaccines and certain immunosuppressive agents. For example, combining adalimumab with abatacept, anakinra, alefacept, or other TNF blockers like infliximab or etanercept increases the risk of serious infections and is contraindicated. Similarly, adalimumab reduces the efficacy of vaccines such as the anthrax vaccine, BCG vaccine, influenza vaccines, and others through pharmacodynamic antagonism, and these combinations are contraindicated. Immunosuppressive therapies, including adalimumab, may interfere with the development of active immunity when administered with vaccines. Caution is advised when combining adalimumab with other immunosuppressive agents, such as cyclosporine, tacrolimus, or sirolimus, due to the increased risk of infections.
